[Last time](../webgpu-two-holes-in-a-wall/) a wave went through a hole in a wall and made a
pattern on the far wall. A single slit made a broad hump. Two slits made fringes. It
looked as if each hole had its own pattern and each one needed working out.

They are all one rule. The pattern a long way behind a hole is the _Fourier transform_ of
the hole. A Fourier transform takes a picture and says how much of each ripple it is made
of: a few broad ripples and a few fine ones, in every direction. A hole is a picture too,
open where the wave gets through and shut where it does not. The wave leaves the hole in
all directions and each direction sees a different ripple of the hole.

On the left below is a hole in a wall, white where it is open. On the right is the pattern
a long way behind it, brightest in the middle. **Paint on the hole with the mouse** and
the pattern follows.

Try these:

- _Two slits._ The same fringes as last time, now with the rest of the pattern. The slits
  are tall and narrow, so the pattern is spread sideways and squeezed up and down.
- _Paint over half of one slit,_ or make a slit fatter. Whatever gets bigger in the hole
  gets smaller in the pattern. A wide hole makes a tight pattern and a narrow one a broad
  pattern.
- _Circle._ A round hole makes rings. It is how a telescope blurs a star.
- _Grating._ Five slits instead of two. The fringes get sharper.
- _Blank,_ then draw anything you like.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| output: false
viewof shape = {
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  return ui.segmented({
    label: "Hole",
    options: [
      ["one", "One slit"],
      ["two", "Two slits"],
      ["grating", "Grating"],
      ["circle", "Circle"],
      ["blank", "Blank"],
    ],
    value: "two",
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| column: screen-inset
//| code-fold: true
//| code-summary: "Show code"
{
  // Shared WebGPU boilerplate: setup, buffers and the animation loop (lib/gpu.js), and
  // the fast Fourier transform (lib/fft.js)
  const gpu = await import(new URL("../lib/gpu.js", document.baseURI).href);
  const fft = await import(new URL("../lib/fft.js", document.baseURI).href);
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);

  // Controls are read live from their elements, so moving them does not restart
  // this cell.
  const shapeInput = viewof shape;
  const brush = 6; // radius of the brush, in cells

  // The hole on the left and the pattern on the right, each 512 by 512 cells
  const N = 512;
  const { canvas, device, context, format } = await gpu.setup({
    width: 1024,
    height: 512,
    resolution: "auto",
  });
  canvas.style.touchAction = "none";

  // The hole: 1 where it is open and 0 where it is wall, kept here and copied across
  const mask = new Float32Array(N * N);
  let area = 0; // how much of it is open
  let painted = false; // true once the shape has been changed by hand
  let dirty = true; // the hole has changed since the pattern was made

  // The slits are tall bars, 80 cells high, with their widths and spacings in cells
  const slitHeight = 80;
  const slits = {
    one: { width: 12, centres: [0] },
    two: { width: 8, centres: [-24, 24] },
    grating: { width: 6, centres: [-64, -32, 0, 32, 64] },
  };

  function shapeMask(kind) {
    mask.fill(0);
    if (kind === "circle") {
      for (let y = 0; y < N; y++) {
        for (let x = 0; x < N; x++) {
          if ((x - N / 2) ** 2 + (y - N / 2) ** 2 < 40 ** 2) mask[y * N + x] = 1;
        }
      }
    } else if (slits[kind]) {
      const { width, centres } = slits[kind];
      for (const c of centres) {
        for (let y = N / 2 - slitHeight / 2; y < N / 2 + slitHeight / 2; y++) {
          for (let x = N / 2 + c - width / 2; x < N / 2 + c + width / 2; x++) mask[y * N + x] = 1;
        }
      }
    }
    painted = false;
    dirty = true;
  }

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------- the transform
  const transform = fft.create(device, N);
  const maskBuffer = gpu.storageBuffer(device, mask);

  // Copy the hole into the transform's input: real part from the hole, imaginary zero
  const loadModule = device.createShaderModule({
    code: `
      @group(0) @binding(0) var<storage, read> hole: array<f32>;
      @group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read_write> data: array<vec2f>;

      @compute @workgroup_size(16, 16)
      fn load(@builtin(global_invocation_id) id: vec3u) {
        if (id.x >= ${N}u || id.y >= ${N}u) { return; }
        let i = id.y * ${N}u + id.x;
        data[i] = vec2f(hole[i], 0.0);
      }
    `,
  });
  const loadPipeline = device.createComputePipeline({
    layout: "auto",
    compute: { module: loadModule, entryPoint: "load" },
  });
  const loadGroup = device.createBindGroup({
    layout: loadPipeline.getBindGroupLayout(0),
    entries: [
      { binding: 0, resource: { buffer: maskBuffer } },
      { binding: 1, resource: { buffer: transform.data } },
    ],
  });

  // ---------------------------------------------------------------------- drawing
  const paramBuffer = device.createBuffer({
    size: 16,
    usage: GPUBufferUsage.UNIFORM | GPUBufferUsage.COPY_DST,
  });
  const cornerBuffer = gpu.unitSquare(device);
  const showModule = device.createShaderModule({
    code: `
      struct Params {
        area: f32,    // how much of the hole is open: the brightest the pattern can be is area squared
        pad0: f32,
        pad1: f32,
        pad2: f32,
      }

      @group(0) @binding(0) var<uniform> params: Params;
      @group(0) @binding(1) var<storage, read> hole: array<f32>;
      @group(0) @binding(2) var<storage, read> spectrum: array<vec2f>;

      struct Out {
        @builtin(position) position: vec4f,
        @location(0) uv: vec2f,
      }

      @vertex
      fn showVertex(@location(0) corner: vec2f) -> Out {
        return Out(
          vec4f(corner, 0.0, 1.0),
          vec2f(corner.x * 0.5 + 0.5, 0.5 - corner.y * 0.5),
        );
      }

      @fragment
      fn showFragment(in: Out) -> @location(0) vec4f {
        let n = ${N}u;
        let y = min(u32(in.uv.y * f32(n)), n - 1u);
        if (abs(in.uv.x - 0.5) < 0.0015) { return vec4f(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0); }

        // The hole, on the left
        if (in.uv.x < 0.5) {
          let x = min(u32(in.uv.x * 2.0 * f32(n)), n - 1u);
          return vec4f(vec3f(mix(0.10, 0.92, hole[y * n + x])), 1.0);
        }

        // The pattern, on the right: the zero frequency is the first element of the
        // transform, so shift by half to put it in the middle
        let x = min(u32((in.uv.x - 0.5) * 2.0 * f32(n)), n - 1u);
        let f = spectrum[((y + n / 2u) % n) * n + (x + n / 2u) % n];
        let intensity = (f.x * f.x + f.y * f.y) / max(params.area * params.area, 1.0);
        // Four decades of brightness, on a log scale
        let t = clamp((log(intensity + 1e-9) / 2.302585 + 4.0) / 4.0, 0.0, 1.0);
        let dark = vec3f(0.10, 0.10, 0.10);
        let red = vec3f(1.0, 0.282, 0.204);   // #FF4834
        let white = vec3f(1.0, 0.95, 0.9);
        let colour = select(mix(dark, red, t / 0.6), mix(red, white, (t - 0.6) / 0.4), t > 0.6);
        return vec4f(colour, 1.0);
      }
    `,
  });
  const showPipeline = device.createRenderPipeline({
    layout: "auto",
    vertex: { module: showModule, entryPoint: "showVertex", buffers: [gpu.squareLayout] },
    fragment: { module: showModule, entryPoint: "showFragment", targets: [{ format }] },
    primitive: { topology: "triangle-list" },
  });
  const showGroup = device.createBindGroup({
    layout: showPipeline.getBindGroupLayout(0),
    entries: [
      { binding: 0, resource: { buffer: paramBuffer } },
      { binding: 1, resource: { buffer: maskBuffer } },
      { binding: 2, resource: { buffer: transform.data } },
    ],
  });

  // ------------------------------------------------------------------ painting
  // Brush strokes go into the hole, on the left half of the canvas
  let painting = false;
  let last = null;
  const place = (event) => {
    const box = canvas.getBoundingClientRect();
    const fx = (event.clientX - box.left) / box.width;
    const fy = (event.clientY - box.top) / box.height;
    return [fx * 2 * N, fy * N];
  };
  function stamp(x, y) {
    const r = brush;
    for (let j = Math.max(0, Math.floor(y - r)); j <= Math.min(N - 1, Math.ceil(y + r)); j++) {
      for (let i = Math.max(0, Math.floor(x - r)); i <= Math.min(N - 1, Math.ceil(x + r)); i++) {
        if ((i - x) ** 2 + (j - y) ** 2 <= r * r) mask[j * N + i] = 1;
      }
    }
    painted = true;
    dirty = true;
  }
  function stroke(from, to) {
    // Stamp along the way so that a fast drag leaves no gaps
    const steps = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(Math.hypot(to[0] - from[0], to[1] - from[1]) / 2));
    for (let s = 1; s <= steps; s++) {
      stamp(from[0] + ((to[0] - from[0]) * s) / steps, from[1] + ((to[1] - from[1]) * s) / steps);
    }
  }
  canvas.addEventListener("pointerdown", (event) => {
    const at = place(event);
    if (at[0] >= N) return; // the pattern side is not paintable
    canvas.setPointerCapture(event.pointerId);
    painting = true;
    last = at;
    stamp(...at);
  });
  canvas.addEventListener("pointermove", (event) => {
    if (!painting) return;
    const at = place(event);
    stroke(last, at);
    last = at;
  });
  const stop = () => (painting = false);
  canvas.addEventListener("pointerup", stop);
  canvas.addEventListener("pointercancel", stop);

  // -------------------------------------------------------------------- the charts
  // The middle row of the pattern (the zero frequency vertically) is the first row of
  // the transform
  const readback = gpu.readback(device, [{ buffer: transform.data, bytes: N * 8 }]);
  let row = []; // {k, I}: brightness along the middle row, relative to the centre
  let needRead = true;

  const [rowHost, costHost] = charts.children;
  const draw = ui.plotter(Plot);

  // What last time's formula gives for these slits: a hump from the width of each slit
  // times fringes from the spacing between them, with k the number of ripples that fit
  // across the 512 cells
  function formula() {
    const kind = shapeInput.value;
    if (painted || !(kind === "one" || kind === "two")) return [];
    const a = slits[kind].width;
    const d = kind === "two" ? slits[kind].centres[1] - slits[kind].centres[0] : 0;
    const rows = [];
    for (let k = -100; k <= 100; k += 0.5) {
      const alpha = (Math.PI * a * k) / N;
      const hump = alpha === 0 ? 1 : (Math.sin(alpha) / alpha) ** 2;
      rows.push({ k, I: hump * (d === 0 ? 1 : Math.cos((Math.PI * d * k) / N) ** 2) });
    }
    return rows;
  }

  function drawRow() {
    draw(rowHost, {
      height: 220,
      x: { label: "ripples across the hole (sideways in the pattern)", grid: true, domain: [-100, 100] },
      y: { label: "brightness (relative to the centre)", grid: true, domain: [0, 1.02] },
      marks: [
        Plot.line(row, { x: "k", y: "I", stroke: "#FF4834" }),
        Plot.line(formula(), {
          x: "k",
          y: "I",
          stroke: "currentColor",
          strokeOpacity: 0.7,
          strokeDasharray: "4 3",
        }),
      ],
    });
  }

  // How long a transform takes to do by the definition and by the fast method, measured
  // here, for a line of n numbers. The definition adds up n terms for each of the n
  // results. The fast method splits the line in two again and again
  function naive(n, re, im) {
    const cos = new Float64Array(n);
    const sin = new Float64Array(n);
    for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      cos[j] = Math.cos((-2 * Math.PI * j) / n);
      sin[j] = Math.sin((-2 * Math.PI * j) / n);
    }
    const outRe = new Float64Array(n);
    const outIm = new Float64Array(n);
    for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) {
      let sr = 0;
      let si = 0;
      for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
        const w = (j * k) % n;
        sr += re[j] * cos[w] - im[j] * sin[w];
        si += re[j] * sin[w] + im[j] * cos[w];
      }
      outRe[k] = sr;
      outIm[k] = si;
    }
    return outRe;
  }

  function fast(n, re, im) {
    re = Float64Array.from(re);
    im = Float64Array.from(im);
    // Put the numbers in bit-reversed order, then join pairs, then pairs of pairs
    for (let i = 1, j = 0; i < n; i++) {
      let bit = n >> 1;
      for (; j & bit; bit >>= 1) j ^= bit;
      j ^= bit;
      if (i < j) {
        [re[i], re[j]] = [re[j], re[i]];
        [im[i], im[j]] = [im[j], im[i]];
      }
    }
    for (let size = 2; size <= n; size *= 2) {
      const step = (-2 * Math.PI) / size;
      for (let start = 0; start < n; start += size) {
        for (let k = 0; k < size / 2; k++) {
          const wr = Math.cos(step * k);
          const wi = Math.sin(step * k);
          const a = start + k;
          const b = a + size / 2;
          const tr = re[b] * wr - im[b] * wi;
          const ti = re[b] * wi + im[b] * wr;
          re[b] = re[a] - tr;
          im[b] = im[a] - ti;
          re[a] += tr;
          im[a] += ti;
        }
      }
    }
    return re;
  }

  const costs = []; // {n, method, us}
  // The best of three, so that a busy moment in the browser does not show up as a bump
  function time(method, n) {
    const re = Float64Array.from({ length: n }, () => Math.random());
    const im = new Float64Array(n);
    let best = Infinity;
    for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 3; attempt++) {
      let runs = 0;
      const start = performance.now();
      do {
        method(n, re, im);
        runs++;
      } while (performance.now() - start < 10);
      best = Math.min(best, ((performance.now() - start) * 1000) / runs);
    }
    return best;
  }
  function drawCost() {
    draw(costHost, {
      height: 220,
      x: { label: "numbers transformed", type: "log", grid: true, domain: [16, 1.1e6] },
      y: { label: "time for one transform (microseconds)", type: "log", grid: true },
      color: {
        legend: true,
        domain: ["by the definition", "the fast way", "the fast way on the GPU"],
        range: ["#FF4834", "currentColor", "#3a9ad9"],
      },
      marks: [
        Plot.line(costs, { x: "n", y: "us", stroke: "method" }),
        Plot.dot(costs, { x: "n", y: "us", stroke: "method", r: 2.5 }),
      ],
    });
  }
  // ------------------------------------------------------------------- the picture
  const readout = ui.readout();

  // How long a transform of a whole picture takes on this GPU, size by size: a batch of
  // them, timed, with the first one thrown away
  async function gpuTime(size) {
    const test = fft.create(device, size);
    const warm = device.createCommandEncoder();
    test.encode(warm);
    device.queue.submit([warm.finish()]);
    await device.queue.onSubmittedWorkDone();
    const runs = 50;
    const encoder = device.createCommandEncoder();
    for (let r = 0; r < runs; r++) test.encode(encoder);
    const start = performance.now();
    device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]);
    await device.queue.onSubmittedWorkDone();
    return (performance.now() - start) / runs;
  }
  let ms = 0;
  for (const size of [32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024]) {
    const t = await gpuTime(size);
    if (size === N) ms = t;
    costs.push({ n: size * size, method: "the fast way on the GPU", us: t * 1000 });
  }
  drawCost();
  readout.textContent = `${N} by ${N} transform: ${ms.toFixed(2)} ms`;

  // Time a size at a time, so that the page is never stuck for long
  (async () => {
    for (let n = 16; n <= 2048; n *= 2) {
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 30));
      costs.push({ n, method: "by the definition", us: time(naive, n) });
      costs.push({ n, method: "the fast way", us: time(fast, n) });
      drawCost();
    }
  })();

  shapeMask(shapeInput.value);
  const on = (element, handler) => {
    element.addEventListener("input", handler);
    invalidation.then(() => element.removeEventListener("input", handler));
  };
  on(shapeInput, () => shapeMask(shapeInput.value));
  drawRow();

  function frame() {
    const encoder = device.createCommandEncoder();
    let sample = false;
    if (dirty) {
      dirty = false;
      area = mask.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0);
      device.queue.writeBuffer(maskBuffer, 0, mask);
      device.queue.writeBuffer(paramBuffer, 0, new Float32Array([area, 0, 0, 0]));
      const load = encoder.beginComputePass();
      load.setPipeline(loadPipeline);
      load.setBindGroup(0, loadGroup);
      load.dispatchWorkgroups(N / 16, N / 16);
      load.end();
      transform.encode(encoder);
      needRead = true;
    }
    if (needRead && !readback.pending) {
      readback.copy(encoder);
      needRead = false;
      sample = true;
    }

    const pass = gpu.beginRenderPass(encoder, context);
    pass.setPipeline(showPipeline);
    pass.setBindGroup(0, showGroup);
    pass.setVertexBuffer(0, cornerBuffer);
    pass.draw(6);
    pass.end();
    device.queue.submit([encoder.finish()]);

    if (sample) {
      readback.read((buffer) => {
        const f = new Float32Array(buffer);
        const centre = f[0] ** 2 + f[1] ** 2 || 1;
        row = [];
        for (let k = -100; k <= 100; k++) {
          const i = (k + N) % N;
          row.push({ k, I: (f[2 * i] ** 2 + f[2 * i + 1] ** 2) / centre });
        }
        drawRow();
      });
    }
  }

  gpu.run(invalidation, device, frame);

  // The canvas with the controls laid over its corner
  yield ui.stage(canvas, [shapeInput, readout]);
}
```

## Analysis

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
//| column: page
charts = {
  // Two empty hosts; the simulation cell above draws into them as data arrives
  const ui = await import(new URL("../lib/ui.js", document.baseURI).href);
  return ui.chartHosts(["row", "cost"]);
}
```

_Left._ The brightness along the middle row of the pattern, for the **One slit** and **Two
slits** holes. The solid line is what the transform gives and the dashed line is last
time's formula for the pattern behind a slit: a hump from the width of the slit and, for
two, fringes from the gap between them. They are the same thing. The formula was the
Fourier transform of a slit, worked out by hand, and here the computer has done it for
every pixel at once. It stops matching as soon as you paint on the hole.

_Right._ How long a transform takes, measured in this browser. The red and grey lines are
a line of numbers on the CPU. By the definition the time grows as the square of the length:
twice as many numbers take four times as long. The fast method takes barely more than
twice as long. At two thousand numbers it is already tens of times quicker and the gap
keeps widening: for a million numbers it would be about fifty thousand to one.

The blue line is the GPU, which transforms a whole picture at once. A 512 by 512 picture
is 262,144 numbers and the GPU does it in less time than the CPU needs for a line of two
thousand. At the small sizes the blue line is above the others, since getting the work
started costs more than the work.

## Gauss, and a Cold War

In about 1805, Carl Friedrich Gauss was working out the orbits of the asteroids Pallas and
Juno from a handful of observations and needed the ripples that the measurements were made
of. He found a way to do it with far fewer sums, wrote it up and did not publish it. It
turned up in his collected works long after his death.

It was found again, more than once. The time it stuck was in 1963 and it was because of
the Cold War. John Tukey was at a meeting of President Kennedy's science advisory
committee, which was talking about how to detect underground nuclear tests from seismometers
placed in the ground. The measurements needed transforms that were too slow to calculate.
Tukey had a way to do them with far fewer sums. Richard Garwin, who was at the meeting,
saw what it could do and passed it to James Cooley at IBM to turn into a program. They
published it in 1965.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Trefethen's 13, no. 1

This is the first paper on [Nick Trefethen's list of 13 classic papers in applied
mathematics](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cme324/classics/): Cooley and Tukey, 1965.
:::

## The shortcut

A line of $N$ numbers $x_j$ has the transform

$$X_k = \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} x_j \, e^{-2\pi i j k / N},$$

which is $N$ sums of $N$ terms each, $N^2$ in all. Split the $x_j$ into the even-numbered
ones and the odd-numbered ones, and each half has a transform of its own, $E_k$ and $O_k$,
that is only $N/2$ numbers long. Putting them back together takes one multiplication each:

$$X_k = E_k + e^{-2\pi i k / N} O_k, \qquad X_{k+N/2} = E_k - e^{-2\pi i k / N} O_k.$$

That joins two half-size transforms into a whole one for the price of about $N$ steps, and
each half can be split the same way, down to lines of one number, which are their own
transform. There are $\log_2 N$ levels of $N$ steps. A million numbers needs about twenty
million steps and not a million million.

## How the computer does it

The pattern is a two-dimensional transform. It is done on the rows and then on the
columns, each of them a line like the one above, so there are $2 \log_2 512 = 18$ passes
over the 512 by 512 grid.

Each pass is the joining step above. One thread on the GPU takes one pair of numbers
and writes out the two they combine to. The passes alternate between two arrays, each one
reading the last one's result and writing into the other, so the numbers come out in order
without a separate shuffle. This form is named for Stockham, and the whole of it is in
`lib/fft.js`. All 262,144 numbers go through each pass at once. The readout under the
canvas is how long the whole thing takes on this machine, measured when the page loaded.

The shader that draws the pattern squares each result to get a brightness and puts it on
a log scale, four factors of ten from the brightest to the dimmest, since the middle is
very much brighter than the edges. The Fourier transform puts the zero frequency in the
corner of the array and the drawing shifts it by half to the middle.

## Sources

- Cooley, J. W. and Tukey, J. W. (1965), "An algorithm for the machine calculation of
  complex Fourier series", _Mathematics of Computation_ 19, 297 to 301,
  [doi:10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1).
- Heideman, M. T., Johnson, D. H. and Burrus, C. S. (1984), "Gauss and the history of the
  fast Fourier transform", _IEEE ASSP Magazine_ 1 (4), 14 to 21.
- IEEE, [First demonstration of the fast Fourier transform, 1964](https://ethw.org/Milestones:First_Demonstration_of_the_Fast_Fourier_Transform_(FFT),_1964),
  for the story of the 1963 meeting.
- Adams, C. S. and Hughes, I. G. (2018), [_Optics f2f: From Fourier to Fresnel_](https://academic.oup.com/book/43688)
  (Oxford University Press), for the pattern behind a hole as a Fourier transform.
